pr_title: fix(core): Allow modification of lifecycle hooks any time before bootstrap
pr_body:
## Overview

Currently we read lifecycle hooks eagerly during `ɵɵdefineComponent`. The result is that it is not possible to do any sort of meta-programing such as mixins or adding lifecycle hooks using custom decorators since any such code executes after `ɵɵdefineComponent` has extracted the lifecycle hooks from the prototype. Additionally the behavior is inconsistent between AOT and JIT mode. In JIT mode overriding lifecycle hooks is possible because the whole `ɵɵdefineComponent` is placed in getter which is executed lazily. This is because JIT mode must compile a template which can be specified as `templateURL` and those we are waiting for its resolution.

## Size tradeoffs
- `+` `ɵɵdefineComponent` becomes smaller as it no longer needs to copy lifecycle hooks from prototype to `ComponentDef`
- `-` `ɵɵNgOnChangesFeature` feature is now always included with the codebase as it is no longer tree shakable.

## Perf tradeoffs
Previously we have read lifecycle hooks from prototype in the `ɵɵdefineComponent` so that lifecycle hook access would be monomorphic. This decision was made before we had `T*` data structures. By not reading the lifecycle hooks we are moving the megamorhic read form `ɵɵdefineComponent` to instructions. However, the reads happen on `firstTemplatePass` only and are subsequently cached in the `T*` data structures. The result is that the overall performance should be same (or slightly better as the intermediate `ComponentDef` has been removed)

## Next steps
- [ ] Remove `ɵɵNgOnChangesFeature` from compiler. (It will no longer be a feature.)
- [ ] Discuss the future of `Features` as they hinder meta-programing.

Fix #30497

⬆️ Please don't kill [component features](https://indepth.dev/component-features-with-angular-ivy/).

Please stop worrying about custom decorators. Custom decorators are experimental and should be treated as such.

The original ECMAScript decorators proposal has been abandoned. There's [a new proposal in early stages](https://github.com/tc39/proposal-decorators), but it has different syntax and semantics.

> Please don't kill [component features](https://indepth.dev/component-features-with-angular-ivy/).

AFAIK it's Angular private API and they can do whatever they want with private APIs.

> Custom decorators are experimental.

Yet they are one of the most widely used TypeScript features and many TypeScript libraries depend on them.

> AFAIK it's Angular private API and they can do whatever they want with private APIs.

It's private now, but because of the phase for stabilization inner structures and finalize the public API. It was always mentioned as the public API at some point.

> Yet they are one of the most widely used TypeScript features and many TypeScript libraries depend on them.

Yep, but it was meant from the official ECMAScript spec point of view.

> Please stop worrying about custom decorators. Custom decorators are experimental and should be treated as such.

Why is everyone fixating on decorators only? The point is, that components are JS classes. Methods on classes are members of prototype. Overwriting a prototype method is an absolutely valid thing to do. Angular currently makes this impossible.

And yes, sure, decorators are one use case of it and I wouldn't make custom decorators for reasons you mentioned, but there are many more use cases.
One use case is a `takeUntilDestroy` which is basically a `takeUntil` that patches `ngOnDestroy` hook in Angular. Impossible right now.

If we can't use custom decorators, you might as well get rid of them across the board in Angular. No `@Input`, `@Output`, `@HostBinding`. I'm not going to keep using a framework if the authors of the framework take a "good for me, but not for thee" approach to something that's a key language feature. Angular originally was going to write its own language just to make decorators possible (Remember AtScript?) and now, because we've got an optimized compiler and some pet private APIs, we're going to say decorators are off limits for end users?

It's not a good look when libraries are built around the idea that developers have to use a subset of a language.
Just FYI, the intention is to review and merge this PR. It is in progress.

@klemenoslaj , you're absolutely right. Currently, we use a custom `takeUntil` implementation which (until Angular 9) added the ngOnDestroy method if it hadn't already been defined in the prototype. Now, I'm having to add a blank `ngOnDestroy()` method to all my components, just for the runtime to recognize that we're using the `ngOnDestroy()` hook. My compiled code has a bunch of useless `KlassComponent.prototype.ngOnDestroy = function() {}` code in it, just to convince the Angular runtime that it's actually using ngOnDestroy. Sure, maybe there's a minute performance boost in the startup time for the application, but my entire bundle has redundant code in it now, so am I really getting a win here?

issue_context.title: Allow custom decorators that use lifecycle hooks in AoT - these are our version of hooks, but we can't use them
issue_context.body:
When writing a custom decorator, lifecycle methods you patch are removed in AoT because the compiler doesn't check that custom decorators are using them.

This results in an inability to create custom decorators with any meaningful component specific behaviour.

React uses hooks to help patch into setup/teardown of your functional components, decorators are Angulars form of hooks. It would be super useful to have this functionality in Angular.
comments:
I have some good news!

In Ivy, lifecycle hooks are purely a runtime concern. They're read off the prototype of the component as soon as the first instance is created, which means that if a decorator adds hooks to the prototype then Ivy will notice them.

@alxhub 

> They're read off the prototype of the component as soon as the first instance is created

This is not true, lifecycle hooks are determined in [`defineComponent()`](https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/e688e02ee442658c754d813e84a9908baf874520/packages/core/src/render3/definition.ts#L266-L272), which happen when the constructor is created, not the instance.

> lifecycle hooks are purely a runtime concern.

However, decorators<super>*</super> are also purely a runtime concern, as explained in https://github.com/angular/angular/issues/16023#issuecomment-425623727, decorators runs after static properties, can be reproduce easily in [TypeScript playground](https://www.typescriptlang.org/play/index.html#src=function%20Custom()%20%7B%0D%0A%09return%20(ctor)%20%3D%3E%20%7B%0D%0A%09%09alert('Decorator%20execution')%0D%0A%09%09return%20ctor%0D%0A%09%7D%0D%0A%7D%0D%0A%0D%0Afunction%20defineComponent()%20%7B%0D%0A%09alert('Static%20property%20execution')%0D%0A%09return%20null%0D%0A%7D%0D%0A%0D%0A%0D%0A%40Custom()%0D%0Aclass%20MyComponent%20%7B%0D%0A%09static%20ngComponentDef%20%3D%20defineComponent()%0D%0A%7D%0D%0A).

When `defineComponent()` get called, all the decorators hasn't being executed yet, so no methods can be found in the `prototype`.

<sub>The [current decorator proposal](https://github.com/tc39/proposal-decorators/) has changed to compile-time semantics, but what implemented in TypeScript is still the obsolete stage-0 proposal.</sub>

@trotyl,

So it looks like this is blocked until Typescript updates the decorator implementation? Which doesn't look like it's in a release plan yet: https://github.com/Microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/Roadmap#future

> So it looks like this is blocked until Typescript updates the decorator implementation?

@ChristopherKiss I really don't know, the decisions are made by Angular team, I have no way to change their mind.

Here is how it should work in Ivy: https://ng-run.com/edit/TIbZM8JylZuhdZCM5KdO

Unfortunately this works only in JIT mode (but fails in AOT mode). The issue is that in AOT mode the `@Component` decorator is converted into `defineComponent` assignment which runs before the decorator has a chance to run. As a result the `defineComponent` collects the lifecycle hooks before the custom decorator has a chance to run.

@mhevery Will this be supported by AOT in the future?
If so, maybe we could take the risk and use `target.ɵcmp` until then.

if `directiveIndex` is `0` than `-0` is a special kind of number which de-optimizes the VM. Where ase `0-0` is always `0`.

Out of curiosity, will Terser try to be smart here and change to `-directiveIndex` anyway?

P.S.: Your answer should probably be a comment in the code because I've seen this question asked elsewhere and I can guarantee people will 'simplify' this in a few months.
I think that we need more tests demonstrating how inheritance works - a test showing override in the middle / bottom of the inheritance chain.

Happy to add a test, but it is not clear to me what I would be testing. The framework logic simply reads the prototype chain. All this refactoring is doing is delaying the reading from eager to lazy. So I don't know what such a test would assert other than that it works the same as normally declared code. Please advise.

I think the rationale in adding tests for this would be that the tests don't know/care that the framework is just reading the prototype; that's just an implementation detail. The tests should verify that the expected behaviors work, even if that would seem "obvious" from the code.

Yeh, my thinking is in-line with @jelbourn - things might be obvious today with the current implementation but not so obvious n months down the line with a modified implementation. Personally I always start to review PRs by reading tests to understand what is the use-case being solved and at this point I have no context / details on the underlying implementation details (nor should have I!).

So yeh, even if it sounds like a super-obvious from the code author point of view, I still think that it would be beneficial to have a test - even if it acts as documentation / non regression. I would even say that we should have test(s) that use a custom decorator and class inheritance to make sure that we really cover the use-case that was reported.
